name: Lena Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Gridline, a small startup that builds energy dashboards for city councils, so they can see which schools and libraries are wasting heat. I'm one of two junior developers, and most days I'm wiring up data from building meters and fixing charts that show nonsense. I talk to the AI assistant all day, honestly, like a very patient senior. Without it I'd be lost, because I came in with a two-year diploma and I'm still behind the others.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that a chart I made helped a council turn down the heating in an empty sports hall. That's real carbon, not a slide deck. What wears me out is the startup chaos, the funding is always six months from running out. Luckily I've saved about seven months of pay, so if Gridline folds I'm not on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a good tool that got sold as a miracle. I'd probably post a slightly smug thread about how the useful part was always the boring part, like explaining errors and drafting tests. At work I'd just keep using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine for me, maybe even good. I've already got the tool habit, so I'd stay a step ahead of people who never picked it up. The real risk to my job is Gridline (the startup she works for) running out of money, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push to own one council's dashboard end to end by next spring. I'd keep using the assistant, and I'd learn the data side properly with a free statistics course. And I'd keep my savings where they are, just in case Gridline folds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small itch. I'd like the world to be a bit more exciting than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the funding is always six months from running out. Does that worry you more than AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much more, yes. Startups die all the time. But there are plenty of developer jobs in the city, so even if Gridline went, I'd be looking for work for a couple of months, not a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tools stay where they are, would you still use them all day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, absolutely. A plateau doesn't make the tool worse. A patient helper that explains my mistakes at midnight is still the best thing that's happened to my learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why workers need a say in how the tools are rolled out. I'd be loud about it: the gains should go into shorter hours, not into fewer of us. And I'd share every guide I've made for using the tools well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a decent spot. I'm the person on the team who already does half my work with AI, so I'd be the one teaching others. But I'm still junior, and if Gridline needs one developer instead of three, I'm not sure it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build an AI agent into our data pipeline at Gridline (her employer), so I'm the person who made the change, not the one replaced by it. I'd do that in the first three months. I'd help start a tech workers' group in the city for small startups. And I'd do a bit of freelance work setting up AI tools for charities on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It's change I can see myself riding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the tools every day. Does that make you safe here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, not safe. The tool makes me faster, but it makes everyone faster. If being good with AI is the new normal, then I'm back to being an ordinary junior with a diploma.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible for the people who don't adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies and the government, together. People shouldn't be blamed for not keeping up with something that moved this fast. I'd want retraining paid for out of what companies save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and pretending otherwise is dangerous. I'd back every proposal for a basic income and public ownership of some of these systems. At work I'd tell the team to plan for the worst and help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my developer job doesn't survive this. If AI can do almost any thinking work better than a person, a junior with a diploma is the first thing it replaces. I don't kid myself about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a solar and heat pump installer course the month this was announced, because I already know the energy side from the dashboards. I'd keep coding at Gridline as long as they'd pay me. And I'd join the campaign for a basic income straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm losing the job, I know that. But I'd have a direction within weeks, and that steadies me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots in 2031. What does that order mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means hands-on work buys me three years after 2028. Installing heat pumps is physical, on roofs and in cellars, and the robots for that come later. It's not forever, but it's something real I'd be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calmer than I'd expect. Are you sleeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. I've got savings, no kids, and plenty of energy. I'd be worried for my mum, who does accounts for a living, more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this fairly, if we start now. I'd push our city tech workers' group to get councils on board with retraining. I'd share my own plan openly, so people can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get maybe three good years in software. That's enough to get properly good, save more, and then move while there's still demand for installers. The timing actually works for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from Gridline to the council's own energy team in year one, which mixes code with site visits. I'd start the installer course part-time in year two. And I'd put an extra tenth of my pay into savings so the switch is painless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a manageable way. I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still go for the installer course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not in a rush. I'd do it part-time and arrive ready, rather than panic-train with everyone else. By 2031 I'd be fitting heat pumps, and the robots for that come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from Gridline's founders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty, mainly. Tell us when they're planning to replace developers with agents. Our founder Ravi is a decent guy, but startups always say everything's fine until payday doesn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we'd better not waste it. I'd be organising, writing, nagging councils. Publicly I'd sound hopeful, because ten years is long enough to build real safety nets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd have a real career first. I'd be 37 in 2036, probably a senior by then, and I'd have savings and choices. The question would be what to do in my forties, not how to pay rent next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Gridline and aim for mid-level in two years. I'd put money into a community solar co-op, because I believe in it and it pays a small return. And I'd keep the tech workers' group going for the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the thinking kind. It's a long way off and I'd have room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you'd do with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd move my savings from the bank into the solar co-op and an index fund. Ten years is long enough for that to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still leave software at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in the end. I'd leave software as someone experienced, maybe managing installation teams, not as a scared junior.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, but mostly for other people. I'd land on my feet, but my mum doing accounts at 55 wouldn't. What would help is free, paid retraining into the energy trades, with a basic income underneath it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people are excited about. I'm a bit scared, sure, but I'm also excited, and I don't think people say that enough.

headlineQuote: I'd land on my feet, but my mum doing accounts at 55 wouldn't.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old** junior developer at a climate-data startup, using AI tools all day.
She sees the assistant as a **patient senior** making up for her two-year diploma.
Progressive and organised, she pushes for **shorter hours** and a basic income.
Her escape route is the **energy trades**, which she knows from her dashboards.
Her **savings** and adaptability keep her calmer than her colleagues, though she expects to leave software.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for people like her **mum**, an accountant at 55.
whatWouldHelp: Free, **paid retraining** into energy trades with a **basic income** underneath.
